content:
From the agentic creators of “The summer of soundness bugs”, and in cooperation with the Lean FRO, we present “The autumn of sound checkers”, episode 1:

I'm happy to announce con-leche.

It is an external lean checker implementation with a consistency proof: If it accepts a set of lean declarations, then they have a set theoretical model (in ZFC with enough inaccessibles). In particular, no theorem of False will be accepted.

It is not particularly fast, but fast enough for real proofs. We ran it on the huge FLT proof by Anthropic, and it worked (it accepted 1044222 declarations at 2 h 22 min wall time and 11 h 38 min task time with a peak RSS of 59.2 GB), and the Navier-Stokes proof is also accepted.

It is written entirely by Claude, with close supervision and regular discussion and guidance from me through prompts. The only human written file in the repository is the README, which may answer some of your questions. The AI written OVERVIEW may answer some more.

We will soon include this as an additional checker in the Kernel Arena, lake check, lean-eval etc. I hope that this will put an end to the worry about large AI formalization possibly abusing kernel implementation bugs.

That said, it is not the end of the journey:

  • I'm proving consistency in a rather blunt way, with a direct set model. I am not proving the checker implementation sound with regard to some abstract ideal typing relation, there is no investigation into meta theoretical properties (e.g. transitivity of defeq, subject reduction, etc.). It also verifies a checker that does additional runtime checks that shouldn't be necessary with a better proof. Therefore I consider it complementary to @Mario Carneiro's lean4lean project, and to all the good type theory research that is happening or planned.
  • It relies on the Lean runtime, which is not covered by the proof, and due to the lack of a soundness proof with regard to an abstract, independent specification, there is still value in having independent checker implementations, in different languages, verified or not. This does not make nanoda or the Kernel Arena obsolete.
  • The proposed renovations to the kernel logic (https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/621470-lean4lean/topic/Lean.20Kernel.20Renovation/with/620267443) are valuable no less and will continue as planned (con-leche anticipates one of then already).

Some background on the making of: I'm technically on unpaid leave since two months for happy family reasons, but I couldn't resist working on things related to the kernel. Out of a doomed attempt at a verifying kernel checker arose lean-inductive-models, and I thought that with the hard technicalities of inductive types handles that way, maybe a verified checker for an extensional core type theory isn't so hard, and I gave it a shot. It wasnt as easy as I thought, and I had to try a few things until Claude and I found a design that was verifiable and fast enough for practical use. I was pretty thrilled when that processed all of mathlib for the first time on Sunday evening. And surprisingly (to me) a “now replace the use of inductive-models for all non-mutual inductives with direct support” was then a one-prompt task of less than a day.

The other observation that I found notable is that I was able to develop this in my free time, essentially on the side, almost exclusively on the phone. It was still a fair amount of work in the end, and the interaction pattern with Claude (checking in very often, redirecting and helping) was certainly less healthy than hour long focused coding in the zone restricted to normal working hours. But I don't think I could have built that otherwise.

I did not scrub the git history or remove the DESIGN document that Claude used to coordinate (and that has grown absurdly large) to be transparent about the making of.

Anyways, I hope you enjoy having your theorems con leche.
So as a clarification, it typechecks something, not necessarily Lean, but that thing is not going to prove False?

It types something that I believe is Lean, just like I believe that nanoda and the official kernel is Lean, and evidence (Kernel Arena tests, real proofs out there) corrobates that assumption. The formal proof does not cover that question, however. That's future work once there is a formal description of what “Lean” is.
Amazing work!
Is there a proof that parsing the input constructs a nontrivial environment, and that conditioned on everything being valid, that environment contains all the declarations from the export file?

No, but it may be in reach: the parser it uses is an agentic hand rolled parser proved equivalent to a naive one, so connecting that to the main proof should be possible. I thought of proving that “if the input string contains these five lines that encode theorem : False then it's rejected, to include the parser in it. Or maybe some form of round trip. But I consider that icing on the cake for now, so no promises.

I guess the adversarial question is, how does one know that it doesn't just produce an empty environment and say "okay everything checks out"? The fact that it actively rejects known "negative" cases from the kernel arena?
Yeah, for example. Or reading that part of the code.
Maybe the next wave of scepticism will be whether the Lean compiler correctly compiled con-leche :)

Absolutely! One of the soundness bugs reported earlier by OpenAI was due to a runtime bug (RC counter overflowing) and one in the bignum implementation. My proof and checker does not help against those, and I would not be surprised if more of those will surface. That's why I point out above that we still need multiple checkers, in different languages.

To be clear, I do not doubt that the checkers are virtuous and truly validate all the input. Rather, to what extent does one need to claim a proof of behavior regarding the final ingested environment?

Because of the issue of semantic alignment, it hasn't been clear to me personally that the veracity of a Lean proof is primarily through the kernel side, although undoubtedly that's a part of it. And to be clear, I appreciate all the work for the checkers and the kernel arena. I'm just curious about those who seek to ask for a verified kernel checker, how "verified" does it need to be?

(Side note, I think a big challenge is in agreeing that _elaboration_ created the statement and semantics we agree on. Maybe we need an elaboration arena)

True, I would like to see better typechecking algorithms in the elaborator. These ought to be more lax to experiment with since the elaborator is not trusted.
As for the degree of verification, con-leche is one step, it will say that you cannot prove a contradiction in the language, but it won't tell me why the thing is true, as there is no typing judgement for one to understand, so basic things like definitional equality won't behave in the way equality is expected to behave, etc. The typing judgement is in essence, the algorithm. But these are not the issues intended to be addressed here, this is in a sense, a quick-and-dirty checker that can give bug-insurance for the spree of large-scale autoformalisations recently, which is still greatly important in this day.
There is a model in set theory. At least to me that's always how I thought about the “why” and “what” of Lean code and proofs, more then the typing judgment. But maybe that's personal taste?
I always thought that producing a set theory model was an act of pettiness by type theorists.

Some quick thoughts without yet looking at the code:

  1. This is amazing!!!!
  2. this needs to be run on Navier Stokes and ideally be added to the standard kernels used by Comparator in things like Palomar.
  3. for GMP calculations @Bas Spitters has a verified version of that in Lean and he has already confirmed it works inside Lean4Lean.
  4. I’d love to see a separation of the spec and the proof of consistency. I’ll right a bit more about what I’m thinking (and I’ve already written other places here about it.). But the main idea is that we can instead of proving consistency directly, prove consistency of the spec which moves all the set model work to one place. The others can reuse the spec (or modify the spec for their interpretation of lean and also modify the set theoretic model.)
  5. This really solidly addresses the worry that Lean’s type theory is not sound by showing there is some interpretation of Lean which is sound and useful. I agree with those above that Talia and others will complain if we don’t prove at least a few more theorems showing this is close to the intended interpretation of Lean? A really nice theorem would be that any statement of arithmetic provable in your model is also true in ZFC + omega inaccessibles. (Or similar with proof about ZFSet but that might be a bit more subtle.) But maybe showing it it’s not vacuous is enough for now.

this needs to be run on Navier Stokes

It is not particularly fast, but fast enough for real proofs. We ran it on the huge FLT proof by Anthropic, and it worked (it accepted 1044222 declarations at 2 h 22 min wall time and 11 h 38 min task time with a peak RSS of 59.2 GB), and the Navier-Stokes proof is also accepted.

@Joachim Breitner I ran some differential testing of con-leche against the official kernel, nanoda, and nanobrujin to find differences in behavior between the kernel implementations. I opened several issues with my findings. Please let me know if this is helpful!

@Jason Rute it's here. I'm still polishing. It's part of my CatCrypt project, I'm hoping to release my compiler soon.
https://github.com/spitters/lean4lean

Jason Rute schrieb:

Some quick thoughts without yet looking at the code:

  1. Thanks!
  2. Yes, done, see message above
  3. Yes, on the agenda, see README, next steps
  4. There are two parts here. One is factoring the proof through a more declarative indictive to be further away from the implementation. Something I may want to do to make the proof easier to follow. The other is to agree on “the” spec, more a social thing and beyond this project.
  5. I thought about proving that “given a formalization of, say, SLTC, con-leche accepts the formalization and then accepts theorems that proves equivalence of terms by reflection and reduction iff the terms are equivalent” or something like that to show that it is not just rejecting everything and actually useful. But not today.

@Joachim Breitner (4) I think we agree about the value of separating the implementation from the more declarative part. As for agreeing on a spec, my worry is that is going to take months and prevent others from making or improving verified checkers. It’s clear there is no agreed upon lean spec and indeed checkers do implement things differently (although I’m not sure if that would lead to different accepted theorems). It is also clear that lean4lean wants a massive overhaul of the lean logic (making def equality transitive and shoring up inductives for example). That is great, but I don’t think it needs to delay projects like this. I instead imagine having a family of specs addressing different interpretations of lean and consistency proofs for them all (when easy).
(5) maybe it is because I was raised in the set/model theory side of logic (even though my advisor is a proof theorist), but it seems to me that showing this model matches standard set theories is the best way to convince others that Navier Stokes and FLT means what you think it means. Also I assume it naturally falls out of your set theoretic model. Maybe I’ll see if I can vibe prove it from your code. But also, in practice your kernel is not rejecting everything (as it accepts FLT and NS), so it probably would be easy to show you are at least accepting small proofs of True and 1+1=2 by running the code in refl, no?

Other thoughts;
(6) how much do you cover the export file format? Could a bad export file (maybe one producible with lean metaprogramming) still allow your kernel to accept a bad result? Or does your proof cover that?
(7) I’m having two conflicting thoughts: One is that projects like this will make it possible to have very heavily optimized kernels. But one avenue of heavy optimization is relying on Lean compiler features, like adding explicit native-decide like checking logic for Booleans which might run into compiler bugs. And just using [implemented by] to speed up code. Do you have thoughts on this and how we can both automatically optimize a kernel but avoid such issues?
(8) what does this code imply about mutual inductives? Does it show they are consistent? Does it convert them to other types but that conversion could fail for some complicated inductives, so it only shows that the fragment which are convertible are consistent? (I thought lean-inductive-models did the latter.)

(8) the latter. It essentially embeds lean-inductive-models for mutual and nested. For mutual out of convenient, it shouldn't be hard to build native support. For nested, maybe claud could even prove that with enough time? We have the translation, why should we not be able to prove that it always succeeds?

Hi everyone!

I'm not an expert on Lean or proof verification, but I am a professional mathematician and am willing to learn. Could the experts here please send some stuff to read, whether existing resources or additional elaboration, about how to understand the meaning of sentences like "So as a clarification, it typechecks something, not necessarily Lean, but that thing is not going to prove False?" or "It types something that I believe is Lean, just like I "believe" that nanoda and the official kernel is Lean, and evidence (Kernel Arena tests, "real proofs out there") corrobates that assumption. The formal proof does not cover that question, however. That's future work once there is a formal description of what “Lean” is."? Similarly, the meaning of the "Why this does not contradict Gödel." sentence in the README?

Thank you so much!
(I'm an assistant professor at Barnard)

In general I think it would be great for the general mathematics community to have additional explanation/discussion about the 'plan' to deal with the many bugs in the lean kernel that the robots seem to easily discover. Perhaps this exists and I don't know where to look, and I'd be happy to advertise it widely if so!

On X, @Talia Ringer brought up another good question that I’ll add to my list above:
(9) Does con-leche depend on the Lean interpreter/compiler more than Lean4Lean? I imagine they both use the Lean runtime bignum arithmetic (and you plan to address that). I assumed otherwise it uses fairly standard compiler features but Talia said:

not sure if there were additional runtime dependencies due to the runtime annotations

It actually depends less on it than Lean4lean. Lean4lean uses Lean’s Lean.Expr which has a bunch of unverifed implementation performance tricks (e.g instantiate has a C++ implementation). con-leche uses none of that, and also no @[implemented_by] (not counting those in the standard library, so some caveat applies).
Will you play Zulip-X-proxy and respond there?

Is it clearly specified somewhere what subset of programs con-leche verifies? (I can imagine one that looks only at programs defining primitive recursive functions, and verifies those. ) Perhaps such a specification can inform what Lean should be.

content: I don’t quite understand: con-leche should accept more or less the same proofs that the offical kernel does (there are some corner cases: it struggles with projections from mutual or nested inductives, but I’m working on it; and it anticipates a change to the transparency of thereom that the official kernel hasn’t done yet)
4 messages were moved from this topic to #AI authored projects > kernel change to theorem transparency by Joachim Breitner.

Small update

I cleaned up the pipeline a bit, as well as the presentation of the main results in the README.

  • The README now exhibits a Main Corrolary (“no proof of False”), but now covers the JSON parser and the annotation pass as well, to give some confidence that these code parts are accessible for verification and not completely bogus (Some parts of the pipeline have much stronger theorems proven about them). The headline corollary is then about a JSON file that encodes, among any other declaration, a theorem _ : False := _.

    Proving more about the complete parser isn’t trivial, and not because of the proof work, but because it’s unclear how to state something more meaningful here. Maybe some round-tripping property or so. But at least we have something about the parser; this is often not done in verification projects.

  • The README also points out the Main Theorem, which is that every accepted environment has a model in the set theory. This was a FAQ: What is con-leches model. This theorem (and the definitions used by it) should be somewhat accessible if you want to convince yourself that what con-leche does has any relation to your expectation and intuition about lean.

I hope you'll find that useful.
Cross-post: con-leche rusted into con-ron: #AI authored projects > con-ron, a Rust port of con-leche with an Aeneas proof

More updates

  • I slightly refactored the proof: Between the actual (pure, unmemoized) core checker code and the “Claims” family of predicates that are already about the set model there is now an inductive predicate that captures the “steps” the checker can do ((the relations in ConLeche/Rules/Rel.lean). This separates operational concerns (e.g. fuel) and heuristics (which side to unfold first etc) from what a checker could do and the consistency proof.

    Notable: the relations have a symm rule for defeq, mostly for proof efficiency (no need to have reduce-left and reduce-right ruels), but no trans rule; that would make the next proof step harder, because of that unconstraint middle term in a trans rule.

  • I improved performance some more, by applying similar tricks that the official kernel does. For example, in a walk over an expr, where caching is crucial to not explode DAGS, we do not bother caching nodes with rc=1. To do this safely in sound code I’m anticipating that a safe withExclusive wrapper around isExclusiveUnsafe is ok and may end up in the standard library.

    Performance-wise its now close to nanoda, processes mathlib in 6min walltime and the fastest non-rust checker on the arena right now. I have removed the “it’s rather slow” wording from the README (it hasn’t been true for a while).
